passage: The cardboard metro train stretched across half the living room of their Kolkata flat. Arnab had been cutting windows for an hour, tongue poking out, glue on his elbow. Kalyani, his older sister, called from the door. "Arnab! The colony drawing contest starts now. There's a trophy!" "In a minute," he said, and didn't move. He was working out how to make the doors slide with a strip of card and a straw. When Kalyani came back, the contest was over. Arnab looked up, surprised it was dark outside. "Didi, look! The doors open!" He didn't ask who had won.

qa.a: She could admire the sliding doors and ask how he figured them out, letting his building time continue instead of pushing him toward the contest.

qa.a: She may feel puzzled or a little frustrated after calling him, but she also gets to see how happy he is when the doors open.

passage: I'm Swati, and last summer I made a whole town out of clay. It was supposed to be for the school craft prize, but I forgot about the prize after the first day. I made a bakery with tiny loaves and a bus stop with a bench. My little brother Yogesh called me for lunch three times. I said "coming" each time and didn't come. Then Amma switched on the light and I saw it was evening. I didn't even enter the contest in the end because I wasn't finished. I don't mind. I still add houses sometimes. Right now I'm making a post office.

passage:
Library note, Friday. Sharmila, school librarian.
Mahima (Class 3) came in for the reading hour and asked for scrap paper. She started a comic about her cat, Pepper, who in the story becomes a pilot. She was bent so close her plait brushed the page.
The bell rang for the quiz in the hall, which has prizes this term. Everyone else left. Mahima didn't hear it. When I tapped her shoulder, she looked up, blinking, and said, "Already? Pepper hasn't landed yet."
She asked if she could stay and finish instead of going for the quiz. I let her.
Next: I will put out a box of drawing paper and some comic books near the window so she knows she can come back.

qa.q: What is the name of Mahima's cat?
qa.a: Pepper.

qa.q: What does Mahima's answer, 'Pepper hasn't landed yet,' show about how she felt?
qa.a: It shows she was so absorbed and happy in her comic that she lost track of time and cared more about finishing it than the prizes.

qa.q: Which choice by Sharmila supported Mahima best, and why?
qa.a: Letting her stay and then setting out paper and comics supports Mahima's own curiosity, instead of pushing her toward the prize quiz.

qa.q: How might Mahima's classmates see her choice to skip the quiz?
qa.a: Some might find it strange that she missed a chance at prizes, not knowing how much the comic itself mattered to her.

grounding: It shows a child so lost in drawing a comic that she forgets time and a prize quiz, a sign of joy in the task itself.

passage:
Sunday
Dear Diary,
Today I opened Nana's old radio. It doesn't work anymore, and Nana said his big boy could, if it stayed unplugged. Urmila Didi lent me her little screwdriver.
Inside it is like a tiny city! Green boards, silver lines, a round thing like a coin. I drew every part in my notebook and gave them names until I learn the real ones.
The colony cricket match was at four. They were giving a trophy. I forgot! Didi came at six and said, "Sumit, you missed the match." I didn't even mind. I found out where the sound comes from. There's a paper cone.
Tomorrow I will ask Sir if there is a book about radios in the school library.
Sumit

qa.q: What did Urmila Didi lend Sumit?
qa.a: Her little screwdriver.

qa.q: Why didn't Sumit mind missing the cricket match?
qa.a: He was so absorbed and excited by the inside of the radio that discovering where the sound comes from mattered more to him than the trophy.

qa.q: What does Sumit plan next, and why is it a good step for him?
qa.a: He plans to ask Sir for a library book about radios, which feeds his own curiosity and helps him learn the real names of the parts.

qa.q: How might Nana feel about Sumit opening his old radio?
qa.a: Nana might feel pleased and proud that the old radio has sparked Sumit's curiosity, since he allowed it as long as it stayed unplugged.

grounding: It shows a child lost for hours in taking apart an old radio, forgetting time and a trophy match because the task itself brings joy and curiosity.

passage:
Sunday
Today I built a whole city out of cardboard boxes. Roads with bottle-cap cars, a hospital, a bridge made from a ruler, and a tower that almost reached the fan.
I started after breakfast. The next thing I knew, Rukmini Didi was standing at the door saying, "Jagdish, it's two o'clock, lunch has been ready for an hour!"
An HOUR. I didn't even hear her call before.
Nobody told me to make it. There's no competition. I just wanted to see if the bridge would hold the bus. (It did, on the third try.)
Didi said I should enter it in the science fair. Maybe. But honestly I just want to add a railway station tomorrow.
– Jagdish

qa.a: Jagdish felt completely absorbed and happy, so curious about the bridge that time disappeared.

qa.a: She might feel amused and impressed, and a little exasperated about lunch.

passage:
In the village near Moga, the afternoon was hot and still. Gurpreet, eleven, sat under the shed with a lump of wet clay from the canal bank.
He began with a tractor. Then a buffalo. Then a tiny farmer with a turban and a water pot. He shaped the fingers with a matchstick, frowning, tongue between his teeth.
Dhruv came running. "Cricket! We're one short!"
"Hmm," said Gurpreet, not looking up.
Dhruv waited. Then he sat down and watched.
The buffalo got horns. The farmer got a moustache. Gurpreet didn't hear his mother calling him for tea until Dhruv nudged him.
"Are you going to sell these at the mela?" Dhruv asked.
Gurpreet blinked. "Sell? I just wanted to see if I could make the moustache."

qa.q: What did Gurpreet use to shape the fingers?
qa.a: A matchstick.

qa.q: What was Gurpreet feeling as he shaped the clay?
qa.a: He felt absorbed and content, curious to see if he could make each detail.

qa.q: What could an adult do to encourage Gurpreet?
qa.a: They could give him time and clay without pushing him to sell or compete, letting the joy in the work lead.

qa.q: How might Dhruv see Gurpreet's clay work?
qa.a: Dhruv seems curious and impressed, forgetting about cricket to watch, and wonders if it could earn money.

grounding: It shows a child absorbed in making clay figures, forgetting time and prizes out of curiosity and joy.

passage:
In the small flat in Cairo, Dalia, nine, sat on the floor surrounded by wires, a battery, and a broken torch she'd found in the drawer.
She wanted the tiny bulb to light up inside a cardboard lighthouse. She tried one wire. Nothing. She twisted it the other way. Nothing. She took the whole thing apart and started again, humming.
Her friend Chen from the floor below knocked. "Are you coming to the park?"
"In a minute," Dalia said.
Chen sat down and watched. An hour went by. The call to prayer drifted in from the mosque; Dalia didn't notice.
Then, click. The lighthouse glowed.
Dalia gasped and laughed. "Look! Look!"
"Is it for school?" Chen asked.
"No," Dalia said, surprised. "It's just for me."

qa.q: What did Dalia want the bulb to light up inside?
qa.a: A cardboard lighthouse.

qa.q: What was Dalia feeling when the lighthouse glowed?
qa.a: She felt joyful and thrilled, laughing after an hour of absorbed effort.

qa.q: How could Dalia's family support this kind of interest?
qa.a: They could give her space, old parts and time to tinker, without turning it into schoolwork or prizes.

qa.q: What is it like for Chen to watch Dalia work?
qa.a: Chen seems patient and curious, waiting an hour and then sharing the surprise when the lighthouse lights up.

grounding: It shows a child absorbed in making a lighthouse, forgetting time and prizes out of curiosity and joy.

The art room at the community centre in Bhopal was open on Saturday mornings. Rehana, nine, came in to draw a picture for a competition.
She forgot about the competition almost at once. She was drawing the old banyan tree outside the window, root by root, twig by twig. She didn't hear the bell for snack. She didn't notice Anjali, the art volunteer, standing behind her.
"Rehana, the entries were due at eleven. It's twelve now."
Rehana looked up, blinking. "Oh." Then she looked back at the roots. "Can I finish it anyway? I just want to see how it looks."
Anjali smiled and pulled up a chair. "Go on. I want to see too."

"There's no prize for this, you know."
"I know," Harsha said. "It's better than a prize."

passage:
"Sachin, you want to know how I became an architect? It started with matchboxes.
When I was a girl of ten, in our small house in Nagpur, I, Aditi, collected every empty matchbox in the lane. One summer afternoon I began building a city with them on the floor. Roads from cardboard, a temple from a soap box.
I built until it was dark. My mother had to step over me to light the lamp. I forgot lunch. I forgot the neighbour's kite competition that I had begged to enter.
When my brother asked, 'Why are you doing this? Nobody will give you a medal,' I didn't even understand the question. It was like breathing. I just wanted to see the city grow.
I think that's where I found myself, beta. Not in marks. On that floor."

qa.q: What did Aditi collect from the lane?
qa.a: She collected every empty matchbox in the lane.

qa.q: How did young Aditi feel while building the matchbox city?
qa.a: She was completely absorbed and joyful, curious to see the city grow, so she forgot lunch and the kite competition.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story when young Aditi chose the city over the kite competition?
qa.a: She stayed on the floor building instead of going to the competition she had begged to enter, following her own curiosity rather than a prize.

qa.q: How might Aditi's brother have seen her building?
qa.a: He was puzzled, thinking there was no point without a medal, not understanding her joy in the task itself.

grounding: An elder recalls being lost for hours in building a matchbox city as a child, forgetting prizes, as the start of her growth.

'Is it for a competition?' Vandana asked. 'No,' said Ganga. 'I just wanted to see if I could draw the rain.'

The blades finally turned in the breeze. Hemant grinned. 'It works!' 'Are you going to enter it in the science fair?' Irawati asked. Hemant looked confused. 'I didn't think about that. I just wanted to see if it would spin.' He ate a laddoo and started taking the windmill apart to make it better.

'In a minute, Vishal Dada!'

Vishal laughed. 'You're missing dinner.'
'Oh.' Chinmay glanced at the clock. 'I thought it was five.'
'It's eight.'
'Can I finish the bus stop first? Just the roof?'
Vishal sighed and sat down beside him. 'Show me how you fold it.'
